entries.title: Introducing Unity Gateway Insights
entries.summary: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models....
entries.content:
Automatically discover inefficiencies in your AI usage

by Adam Gurary, Alkis Polyzotis and Vishnu Kannan

When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing. 

Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights, which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data.

If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions:

  • What are people working on? Insights compares each workstream's share of sessions with its share of tokens. A workstream with 10% of sessions and 35% of tokens is the first place to look.
  • Where can I save money? Insights shows where tokens go and ranks each kind of waste by what it costs. For each repeated workflow, Insights writes a prompt you can copy to turn that workflow into a shared skill.

Each finding links to example sessions, so you can open the traces behind it.

You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send.

Here's what's behind each kind of waste Insights reports:

  • MCP Errors & Waste: When a tool call fails, agents retry or work around it until the task gets done, so the session looks like it worked while you pay for every retry. The $1.2M we found came from just seven small bugs in our MCP servers: $499K in wasted tokens plus 12,000 hours of engineers waiting on agents. Fixing all seven took about an hour.
  • Inefficient Model Usage: Insights rates how complex the task was in each frontier-model session and counts the quick, routine ones, along with the tokens they used. Those are the sessions Smart Routing can send to a cheaper model while keeping frontier models for the work that needs them.
  • Common workflows to codify: A workflow counts when it recurs in at least three sessions or across two engineers. A shared skill gives agents those steps up front, so you stop paying for them to work the steps out again every session.

Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them.

Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. It depends on four things a standalone gateway can't have:

  • Every agent traced automatically. Unity Gateway is the control plane your coding agent requests go through. When engineers launch Claude Code, Codex, or GitHub Copilot with the ug CLI, ug turns on each agent's own OpenTelemetry tracing automatically, so your teams have nothing to instrument. Traces land in the unified trace table, a governed Delta table in Unity Catalog that you own, in an open format any tool can read.
  • Genie that knows your business. Genie writes the SQL and reads the sessions. With Genie Ontology, its answers use your own project names and business nuances.
  • Scale for millions of traces. Databricks SQL queries your full trace history with the same scale and performance it brings to your largest tables.
  • Locked down by default. Traces hold prompts, code, and tool output, so only the table's owner can query it until admins grant access with Unity Catalog grants and row filters. Insights reads the table in place, so you never export your most sensitive data to analyze it.

If your developers already run coding agents through Unity Gateway, you can generate your first report today:

  • Set up the unified trace table so Unity Gateway records traces.
  • Have your teams launch their coding agents with the ug CLI.
  • In your workspace, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report. See the Insights documentation for details.

entries.title: What's new for Genie in Microsoft: Copilot Cowork and Chat, Microsoft Teams, and Excel.
entries.summary: Most AI assistants can read a person's email, files, and calendar, but it can't tell...
entries.content:
The Azure Databricks Genie plugin brings governed Azure Databricks context to Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft Copilot Cowork, alongside Genie in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Excel.

by Kiriana Stukas and Toussaint Webb

  • Genie works in the Microsoft tools you already use: Genie is available in Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Teams, Excel, and Copilot Studio.
  • Genie in Microsoft Teams is generally available: DM the Databricks Genie app or @mention it in a channel or group chat to get governed insights without leaving Teams. The same app also works in Microsoft 365 Copilot.
  • Governed answers in Microsoft Cowork, in a few clicks: The Azure Databricks Genie plugin connects Genie One to Microsoft Copilot Cowork and chat, so users get governed insights from across their data estate.

Most AI assistants can read a person's email, files, and calendar, but it can't tell which revenue table is certified or how finance defines net retention. This leads to inconsistent outcomes, low adoption, and a lack of trust among business users. Genie Ontology solves this context problem for Genie by combining the business semantics teams explicitly define with context learned from everyday work, so answers are grounded in a full understanding of the business.

Once that context is unified, the next step is putting it to work. As AI assistants and agents spread across the business, organizations need to control data access, spend, and tool usage at scale. Without that control, sensitive data can reach the wrong people, AI spend becomes hard to predict, and agents can connect to tools no one has approved. In Genie, Unity Catalog enforces each user's data permissions, and Unity Gateway gives admins the traces, MCP policies, and budget controls they need to manage AI across the organization.

Genie brings both essential context and governance into the Microsoft tools your teams already use with the Azure Databricks Genie plugin, which connects Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Cowork to Genie One. Genie also works in Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Excel, and Microsoft Copilot Studio.

The Databricks Genie app for Microsoft Teams is now generally available, bringing Genie into the conversations where teams already make decisions. Users can send Genie a direct message or mention @Databricks Genie in a channel or group chat, and Genie replies in the thread with answers grounded in the organization’s governed business context.  

With Genie in Teams, users unlock real-time collaboration with knowledge from across their data estate. For example, a sales manager can post in a channel, "Which open leads over $100K haven't had a follow-up this week?" Instead of someone manually pulling the pipeline report, cross-checking it against the CRM, searching meeting notes, and messaging reps one by one, she can now simply tag @Genie. Genie answers in the thread with the matching leads, their latest activity, and links to the sources it used, not only saving the team time and effort, but also allowing the work to happen right where the question was originally asked.

Genie in Teams goes beyond answers, enabling users to turn insights into work right from their Teams workspace:

  • Schedule recurring analyses: Click “Run this analysis on a schedule” under an answer, or ask in your own words, for example "send me this analysis every Monday at 9 AM." Results arrive in your DM.
  • Work with files: Attach a file for Genie to analyze, and get documents such as PDFs back in the thread.
  • Share charts in a thread: Genie returns visualizations directly in Teams, so the chart is ready when your team needs it.

The Azure Databricks Genie plugin for Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Copilot Chat brings trusted business answers into the Copilot experience users may already rely on. Instead of Copilot searching for correct answers on its own, it can delegate work to Genie One. Genie leverages Genie Ontology to provide accurate insights based on certified definitions, metric views, and context learned from everyday work, all governed by Unity Catalog. 

Together, Genie and Copilot can unlock new workflows for teams. For example, imagine an account team preparing for client meetings. An account director asks Copilot Cowork for a briefing ahead of a customer meeting, which delegates to Genie. Genie pulls usage, spend, and account trends from Azure Databricks using certified metric definitions, then reads recent customer email threads in Outlook through its Microsoft 365 connector to flag open escalations. Cowork turns those insights into a Word doc brief, an Excel overview with charts, and a client-ready presentation. Every figure comes from Genie, keeping the deliverables consistent with the numbers finance and the account team already report.

Many teams plan, forecast, and report in Excel, but getting trusted data into a workbook often means exporting files, copying numbers, and hoping they match the source. With Genie One in the Azure Databricks Excel Add-in, analysts can ask questions in plain English and get answers from governed Azure Databricks data without hunting for tables or writing SQL. Every answer includes citations that show where the numbers came from, and analysts can refine their analysis with follow-up questions, resume past conversations, and load table results directly into the workbook for further modeling.

The Excel Add-in also lets teams:

  • Build live pivots on Unity Catalog metric views and tables. Results populate as fields are dragged in, with no refresh button.
  • Schedule refreshes so recurring reports, forecasts, and scorecards stay current with the latest data.
  • Write back finalized inputs, such as forecast assumptions or planning updates, to Databricks tables.

Together, these capabilities bring governed Azure Databricks data into the spreadsheet workflows teams already rely on, without exports or manual data movement.

Builders can connect Genie Agents to Microsoft Copilot Studio using the Azure Databricks connector for Power Platform. Adding Genie as a tool lets a Copilot Studio assistant delegate questions about Azure Databricks data to Genie Agents, which answer using curated data and instructions and governance enforced by Unity Catalog.

Business questions rarely stay in one tool, so the answers shouldn't either. Together, Microsoft and Genie bring governed business context from Azure Databricks into the tools every employee already uses: Copilot Chat, Copilot Cowork, Teams, and Excel. Genie Ontology makes sure every answer is grounded in your enterprise context, and Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway enforce governance for every answer and action. Now, wherever a question starts, whether in a Teams thread, a Copilot chat, or an Excel workbook, users get the same trusted, governed answer.

What is Genie Ontology? 

Genie Ontology is the enterprise context layer that gives Genie and other AI agents a shared understanding of your business. Agents build it from everyday work, people govern it, and every agent can use it. It combines business semantics that teams define, such as metric views and certified definitions, with context learned from dashboards, queries, and documents. Genie Ontology is now generally available.

How does Genie Ontology help Microsoft Copilot give better answers? 

It gives Copilot the business meaning behind the data. When Copilot or Copilot Cowork asks Genie a question, Genie answers with the certified definition, such as how finance defines net retention, instead of guessing from table names. Teams get consistent answers in every Microsoft tool.

How do admins govern Genie across Microsoft tools? 

Through Unity Gateway. Admins manage AI usage centrally with MCP policies, cost controls, and monitoring. MCP policies decide which MCP servers and tools Genie can use, who can access them, and which actions need human approval. Traces record what Genie did and who asked for it.

How do I get started with Genie in Microsoft Teams?

Admins add the Databricks Genie app to Microsoft Teams and choose the default visibility for responses. Users then send Genie a direct message or mention @Databricks Genie in a channel or group chat. The first time, they sign in to Databricks and pick a workspace.

Does Genie in Teams support Genie One and Genie Agents? 

Yes. Genie One is the default. It looks across your entire data estate to answer each question. You can also pin a conversation or channel to a specific Genie Agent. Questions are then sent to that agent through the Genie Agentic API, so answers stay scoped to that agent's curated data and instructions.

What can Genie do in Microsoft Teams? 

Genie in Teams does much more than answer questions. You can:

  • Discover and visualize insights: Get answers, tables, and charts from your Databricks data in a direct message or channel.
  • Search your company's knowledge: Pull in context from connected sources.
  • Take action in other tools: Create or update a document, comment on a ticket, or update a record through MCP connectors. Genie asks for your approval before it makes a change.
  • Schedule recurring analyses: Run an analysis on a schedule and get the results in your DM. To set up, ask Genie to "Send me this analysis every Monday at 9 AM."
  • Work with files: Attach PDF, Word, or CSV files for Genie to analyze, and get documents such as PDFs back.
  • Pick the right expert: Use Genie One across your whole data estate, or pin a conversation or channel to a specific Genie Agent.
  • Give feedback: Rate answers with a thumbs up or down to help improve Genie.

Does Genie in Microsoft Teams support workspaces that use Private Link? 

Yes. A Databricks account admin needs to create a context-based ingress policy to allow secure connectivity between Teams and your Databricks workspace.

Is my data secure for Genie in Microsoft Teams? 

Yes. Every question runs as the user who asked it, so Genie only uses data that person is allowed to see, based on Unity Catalog and source permissions. Questions are processed inside your Databricks workspace. The service that routes messages between Teams and Databricks doesn't store questions or answers.

Should I use the Databricks Genie app in Teams, or publish a Copilot Studio agent to Teams?

Use the Databricks Genie app in Microsoft Teams by default. It's a native app that chats directly with Genie One, so users get answers from across their data estate with no extra agent in between. It also works in Microsoft 365 Copilot. The app supports pinned Genie Agents, charts, file uploads, and MCP actions, and it doesn't require a Copilot Studio license. Choose Copilot Studio when you're building a custom agent that combines Genie Agents with other tools not available within Azure Databricks.

How do users get started with the Azure Databricks Genie plugin?

Users can get started in a few clicks. In Copilot Cowork, they turn on the Azure Databricks Genie plugin, click Connect, and sign in with their Azure Databricks credentials. The plugin doesn't require an OAuth app registration or manifest edits.

Which Microsoft tools work with Genie?

Genie works across Copilot Chat, Copilot Cowork, and Microsoft 365 apps. It's also available in Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Power Platform, and Microsoft Agent 365. Genie One in Microsoft Foundry brings the same governed context to agents built in Foundry.

How does Genie work with Microsoft Foundry?

Genie works with Microsoft Foundry in both directions. Agents built in Foundry can use Genie One to get governed Azure Databricks data while acting as the signed-in user. Microsoft Foundry models are also available in Azure Databricks through Unity Gateway.

Can Genie connect to Work IQ over MCP?

Genie will soon connect to Work IQ over MCP, through Model Context Protocol, so organizations that use Work IQ can bring Microsoft 365 context into Genie alongside governed Azure Databricks data. That context includes email, meetings, documents, Teams messages, and people and organizational context. Each request runs under the signed-in user's Microsoft Entra ID identity, so Microsoft 365 permissions, sensitivity labels, and compliance policies continue to apply while Unity Catalog governs the Azure Databricks data.

entries.title: How AUMOVIO centralized AI access with Databricks Unity Gateway
entries.summary: As AI adoption grew, AUMOVIO teams developed different ways to access large language...
entries.content:
by Louis Rottmeier, Maximilian Fest, Michael Boesl, Michael Weber, Martin Gindler and Kelly Albano

As AI adoption grew, AUMOVIO teams developed different ways to access large language models. Today, Databricks Unity Gateway provides a shared entry point for our AI workloads. This blog discusses how we brought these approaches together.

Teams at AUMOVIO developed different ways to access LLMs, including provider integrations and gateways built for specific use cases. These approaches all addressed real needs, but as AI adoption grew, their variety added complexity to operations, cost attribution and consistent governance.

The main opportunities to improve were:

  • Shared visibility. Bring model usage into one place for consistent reporting.
  • Cost transparency. Attribute spend to a user, team or use case.
  • Simplified operations. Manage provider updates, incidents and support through a shared service.
  • Consistent governance. Apply model approvals, logging and guardrails through a common approach.

Together, these approaches highlighted the value of a shared operating model for managing our AI workloads with a single AI gateway solution

AUMOVIO's cross-functional AI taskforce brought together stakeholders from security, data protection, business areas and IT. The taskforce decided on one central AI Gateway as the shared route for LLM access and governance, establishing a common direction for model access across the company.

From there, our job was to make the central path useful to teams and their applications.

Building an AI gateway is straightforward, but operating one as an enterprise service is a permanent commitment: provider APIs change, dependencies need patching, security requirements evolve, and users need support. Once applications depend on it, a gateway needs a roadmap, an on-call rotation and a support process. Weighing that against buying yet another AI gateway, five arguments decided why Databricks Unity Gateway was the solution for us.

1. Databricks was already our data platform. 1ADP, the One AUMOVIO Data Platform, runs on Databricks. Putting model access next to our governed enterprise data meant no new vendor, no new network path to review and no isolated stack to operate.

2. Corporate identity integration. Databricks is integrated with our corporate Microsoft Entra ID tenant, and other AUMOVIO applications authenticate against that same tenant. An application presents its Entra ID token and gets access to Unity Gateway through token exchange, with no separate account, no API key to distribute and no bespoke integration. Onboarding a new AI-enabled application takes a permission grant, and access to every model ends automatically when the corporate identity does.

3. Governance and usage tracking. Model approvals, access policies, usage tracking and logging sit in one place instead of being reimplemented per application. Payload logging through inference tables is off by default and only enabled with an explicit, approved justification, which is the posture our data protection agreements require.

4. We stayed free to choose providers. This mattered most. We publish a curated catalog of 1adp-* model aliases, and Unity Gateway routes each alias to whichever provider serves it: Databricks-hosted foundation models, Google Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock or others. Users code against a stable, vendor-neutral name, and we can re-point that name to a different provider or a newer model without a single consumer changing a line of code. The aliases give teams a consistent route to approved models.

5. The setup is infrastructure as code. Terraform expresses everything Unity Gateway does for us: the endpoints behind each 1adp-* alias, the provider each model routes to, the fallback order when a provider degrades, rate limits and the guardrails applied per endpoint. Adding a model, re-pointing an alias or tightening a safety control is a pull request, reviewed, versioned and reproducible across environments. When production misbehaves, our version control explains the configuration that caused it. Because we provision the rest of 1ADP the same way, the Gateway is one more module for the engineers who already run the platform.

Centralizing model access was the first step. We then built three capabilities on top of Unity Gateway to support how our teams manage, access, and use AI:

Cost attribution and chargeback. Unity Gateway reports on how many tokens were consumed, and every user assigns their consumption to a personal cost center or to one of the projects they work in. Pipelines join that assignment with Databricks system tables and charge usage to the right cost center. We publish the result as dashboards: which models are used, by whom, how consumption develops and what it costs. Budget owners can see their spend and identify changes in consumption.

A curated model catalog. Standardized access does not make models interchangeable. The catalog is the single source of truth for which models are approved, what they map to and which consumption tier they run in. Teams still test their application against the model they choose, but they no longer build infrastructure to reach it.

An interface for employees. The 1ADP AI App runs in production on the same gateway and gives employees a governed way to use AI without writing code. Developers get an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and can point compatible agentic coding tools at the central models. Same infrastructure, two audiences: we standardize model access and leave the choice of development interface open.

Unity Gateway provides a shared route for LLM access. The 1adp-* aliases connect applications to models, guardrails apply centrally, and usage is attributed to cost centers in near real time.

The next phase moves up the AI platform stack: sharing agents inside 1ADP projects and connecting knowledge sources, web search and other tools through managed and bring-your-own MCP (Model Context Protocol) connections. Model access stays centralized; what changes is the range of tools an agent can reach. That raises questions about what an agent may retrieve, which tools it may call and whose permissions it acts under. Having one framework to answer them in is why we consolidated in the first place.

If you are bringing different model access approaches together, involve security, data protection, business areas and IT in the operating model. Then make the shared service useful to the teams expected to use it.

When you compare building to buying, price the decade rather than the prototype. Ask who patches the provider integration, who answers the support ticket, who handles the incident, and who does it again next year.

Then decide what is genuinely yours to build. The gateway was not. Cost attribution, the model catalog and the employee-facing AI App were, because they encode how AUMOVIO works and no vendor was going to hand them to us.

We remain accountable for our architecture, our security decisions and the quality of our applications. Unity Gateway provides the shared model access service, while teams can continue to choose the applications they build.

AUMOVIO chose Databricks Unity Gateway to centralize AI model access without the ongoing maintenance, security updates, and operational overhead of building its own gateway. Because Databricks already powered its enterprise data platform, AUMOVIO could reuse existing infrastructure, Microsoft Entra ID integration, and governance controls. This allowed its teams to focus on building company-specific capabilities such as cost attribution, a curated model catalog, and an employee-facing AI application.

Databricks Unity Gateway provides a single, governed entry point for accessing AI models across providers such as Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock, and Databricks-hosted models. AUMOVIO uses centralized model approvals, access policies, logging, and guardrails to apply consistent governance across applications. Its curated model aliases also let administrators change the underlying model or provider without requiring application code changes.

Unity Gateway provides token usage data that enterprises can use to track AI consumption across models and users. AUMOVIO combines this data from Databricks system tables with project and cost center assignments to attribute AI spending to the appropriate business owners. Dashboards provide near-real-time visibility into model usage, consumption trends, and costs, supporting internal chargeback and budget oversight.

Databricks Unity Gateway provides centralized model access through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, reducing the need for developers to manage separate provider integrations. At AUMOVIO, applications authenticate through Microsoft Entra ID token exchange, eliminating the need to distribute individual API keys. Developers can use approved models through compatible coding agents and applications while IT manages permissions and provider connections centrally.

A centralized AI gateway simplifies access to multiple models while bringing governance, cost visibility, and operational management into one shared service. AUMOVIO uses Unity Gateway to support both employee-facing AI applications and developer tools through the same infrastructure. Its next phase will extend this approach to shared AI agents and MCP connections, with a focus on governing tool access and permissions.

entries.title: How we raised Databricks cluster rate limits by 7.5×
entries.summary: As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure...
entries.content:
Why adaptive concurrency limits work better than fixed request-rate limits for long-running operations.

by Heqing Ya, Tan Zhang, Ankit Batra and Abhishek Rai

  • Adaptive concurrency limits track long-running cluster-creation workflows and adjust how much work can run as system health changes.
  • Bounded queues and fair scheduling help absorb bursts and share capacity. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains a customer-facing guardrail.
  • Databricks raised default cluster-creation request-rate limits by 7.5× and removed over a hundred customer-specific overrides in the reported scope.

As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure into clusters ready to run customer workloads. Our day-to-day work includes provisioning virtual machines and coordinating cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Our goal is to keep these systems available while letting customers use as much capacity as we can safely provide.

In this post, we'll explore why fixed request-rate limits can fall short for these long-running operations, how adaptive concurrency limits help, and what we learned applying them to cluster creation for Databricks classic compute. You don't need to know any of this to use Databricks, but if you're curious about what happens behind a Databricks Runtime cluster launch, join us for a look inside the kitchen.

Historically, we protected the system with fixed request-rate limits, tested against different load patterns and failure scenarios. We scaled our services primarily by adding resources and adjusting per-customer limits.

The combination of workloads and dependency failures made these limits increasingly difficult to test and tune. Conservative limits turned away customer requests despite spare capacity, yet kept accepting requests when our services or dependencies, such as cloud providers, slowed down. Engineers manually lowered limits to shed load during incidents and raised them again after recovery.

Adaptive concurrency limits account for both unfinished work and changing system health. They let more work start when capacity is available and slow the pace when the system struggles, helping the service make progress with less manual tuning. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains as a final safety guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic.

Think of our compute platform as a kitchen, aiming to serve as many orders as its cooks and equipment can handle. The manager posts a fixed rule: accept at most ten new orders per minute, whatever is happening at the stove.

Even with spare cooking capacity, the rule turns orders away. When an oven breaks, it keeps accepting orders faster than the remaining cooks and equipment can finish them. The manager has to keep rewriting the sign each time.

A better kitchen keeps a short queue and limits how many meals are being prepared at once. If an oven breaks, fewer meals start; as capacity returns, more can begin. Orders can wait briefly, but only while there is still time to serve them.

For long-running operations, a fixed request rate is a poor model of capacity. The goal is to let customers run at full throttle when capacity allows, then ease off enough to keep useful work moving during degradation.

An API call can launch much more work than the handler performs itself. For cluster creation, the handler validates the request, records a work item, and returns. A background workflow coordinates services, updates state, and provisions resources such as cloud virtual machines. These operations complete asynchronously, and their duration depends on the health and capacity of their dependencies. The API call may take milliseconds; the workflow itself may take minutes.

A request-rate limiter at the API entry point caps requests per time window. That is useful for enforcing quotas, preventing abuse, and protecting the resources used to handle API calls.

A fixed request-rate limit is easier to tune when available capacity and the work behind each request stay reasonably predictable. Cluster creation makes both difficult: one request may provision a few VMs and another many more, while cloud-provider health changes how long provisioning takes. During a shared slowdown, many workflows take longer at the same time. The same incoming request rate can therefore leave much more work in flight, even as the system’s ability to finish it falls.

On the left, arrivals stay fixed at one operation per time unit. Increasing duration from two to six time units triples the work in flight. On the right, processors become slow or unavailable, reducing the capacity available to handle that work.

When a dependency degrades, more calls fail or time out. Long-running workflows retry those calls to recover from temporary faults. Across many active workflows, those retries add pressure to the struggling dependency, causing more failures and yet more retries—a retry storm.

These internal retries come from work already accepted, so the API request-rate limiter does not see them. They can sustain overload even after incoming traffic returns to normal. Limiting active workflows helps contain that pressure and gives unfinished work a chance to drain.

Setting a lower rate does not solve the mismatch. It buys headroom by rejecting more work during healthy periods, and a large enough slowdown can still exhaust that headroom. Raising the rate makes better use of healthy capacity but accepts more work during degradation. One number has to cover both days.

“Rate limiting” is sometimes used broadly to include limits on concurrent work. Here, we distinguish the two mechanisms by what they count.

Term Meaning in this article
Operation The full workflow, including background work after the API returns.
Request-rate limit A cap on requests accepted per unit time, such as 10 requests per second, with a possible burst allowance.
Concurrency How many operations are active at once, including those waiting on dependencies.
Concurrency limit A cap on active operations, such as 100 at once. Each operation holds a slot until it finishes.
Backlog Accepted work waiting to start; it has not acquired an active slot yet.

Either kind of limit can be fixed or adaptive. Our comparison is between fixed request-rate limits and adaptive concurrency limits for protecting long-running work.

The kitchen needs to track meals still being prepared and the capacity available to finish them. In Databricks classic compute, the equivalent is the set of cluster-creation workflows still provisioning infrastructure. We give each active workflow a slot and adjust the number of slots as conditions change.

Consider a CreateCluster request for a cluster with a driver and several worker VMs. Once the request is accepted, its provisioning workflow waits for a slot before it starts. We track whether that work is queued, actively processing, or complete.

If all slots are occupied, the request stays queued. An active workflow keeps its slot while it provisions VMs and waits for dependencies. Once the workflow finishes, its slot becomes available for another cluster launch. A successfully launched cluster can keep running customer workloads for hours without occupying that provisioning slot.

The slot must cover the whole provisioning operation, including background work after the API returns. Tracking a slot does not require holding a thread.

This controller counts active provisioning workflows. Running clusters, allocated VMs, and vCPUs are separate measures. One workflow can provision many VMs, so one slot does not imply a fixed resource cost.

Now suppose a cloud provider takes longer to provision VMs. Active workflows hold their slots longer, so new cluster launches start less often even if the slot limit stays fixed. Customers see longer launch waits as accepted requests queue.

Adaptive control also changes the slot limit. For cluster creation, useful signals include how long provisioning takes and whether critical thread pools are saturated. When these signals indicate congestion, the controller reduces the number of concurrent provisioning workflows. As conditions recover, it cautiously allows more. Capacity pressure changes when accepted work starts; RPC rate-limit rejections are reserved for exceptionally high incoming request rates.

Reducing the limit prevents new operations from starting until active work falls below it; existing operations still need time to finish. This response time matters when workflows last minutes. Retries also need backoff and a limit on attempts so active workflows do not keep overwhelming a recovering dependency. Concurrency limiting cannot repair an unavailable dependency, but it can limit the extra pressure while that dependency recovers.

The control loop answers how much work to start. Building a useful service also means deciding who waits, how long they wait, and what we tell them.

“Too many requests” can hide two very different situations.

In the first, a customer sends its usual traffic, but a shared dependency slows down. Capacity has fallen. Asking the customer to fix its traffic pattern misattributes a service problem.

In the second, a customer submits an unusually large burst while the service remains healthy. Other customers are competing for the same resources. Throttling that burst protects their fair share.

To tell these cases apart, track system health, each tenant’s incoming demand, and the scheduling decision separately. A large number of in-flight operations alone does not prove that a customer sent too much: those operations may be stuck behind a slow dependency. Likewise, a burst need not be throttled for fairness if spare capacity is available and policy permits it.

This distinction belongs in metrics and customer-facing explanations. It tells operators whether to investigate lost capacity or an unusual workload, and tells customers whether changing their behavior will help. Count failures caused by service degradation in service reliability metrics, even when they surface as throttling. For accepted requests that wait in the queue, measure the impact on cluster launch latency.

For an operation that takes minutes, a short wait is often preferable to an immediate error followed by a retry. A queue can absorb a burst and let the system catch up.

That only works if waiting fits the request’s deadline. Bound the queue’s size and each request’s waiting time, make progress visible, and reject or expire work when it can no longer finish usefully. A queue cannot turn sustained overload into capacity; an unbounded one can turn a brief disruption into hours of delay.

A queued request should be a small record, not a running worker holding scarce resources. A larger backlog should not make every active operation more expensive through repeated scans or competition for threads and connections.

Cleanup needs the same attention. If a large backlog expires together, the service must be able to discard it within a predictable time. Plan for the worst backlog, keep expiration and rejection cheap, and avoid doing expensive setup for work whose deadline has already passed. Otherwise, the queue can keep the service busy long after the original congestion has ended.

Suppose a service must delay a hundred requests. Is it better for a hundred customers to each see one slow request, or for one customer to see a hundred slow requests?

The aggregate metric may look the same. The customer experience will not.

A scheduler makes this choice whether we specify it or not. Define which work should go first, what share each tenant should receive under contention, and how lower-priority work avoids waiting forever. Let tenants use otherwise idle capacity where the policy allows it, while preserving fair access when other tenants need their share.

We applied these ideas to an integrated load management system for cluster creation on Databricks classic compute. A short API request starts a much longer workflow that coordinates several dependencies, including public clouds, to provision compute resources.

The system combines queued requests, adaptive concurrency limits, and fair scheduling. It uses the work already in flight and system health to decide when queued operations can start.

We kept the API request-rate limit as a final line of defense against exceptionally high incoming traffic. It provides a request-rate boundary we can communicate to customers. Adaptive concurrency limits stay inside the service and govern when accepted work starts. A successful API response does not guarantee an immediate cluster launch or completion within a fixed time.

The initial rollout analysis reported three outcomes:

  • 7.5× higher default cluster-creation request-rate limits.
  • More than 99.99% fewer cluster-creation rate-limit errors in the reported scope.
  • Over a hundred customer-specific rate-limit overrides in scope removed.

Adaptive concurrency control made the 7.5× increase possible by protecting the long-running workflows as conditions changed. Since that increase, few customers have hit the higher cluster-creation request-rate limits, and we have added no new manual overrides for those limits. Customers have more room to scale, with less need for individually tuned exceptions.

Applying this approach to other kinds of long-running work raises further design questions. When operations have very different resource costs, counting each as one slot may be too coarse; weighted slots or separate limits are possible extensions. For workflows with several bottlenecks, another design question is where to apply control so a slow dependency does not hold up unrelated work.

During a cloud-provider slowdown, workflows already provisioning VMs can keep retrying even after new launches slow down. Pair concurrency limits with retry backoff and a limit on attempts to reduce that pressure during recovery.

A request-rate limit caps how many requests are accepted per unit time; a concurrency limit caps how many operations are active at once. Each active operation holds a slot until it finishes, including time spent waiting on dependencies.

A CreateCluster workflow holds its slot while provisioning VMs, including time spent waiting on dependencies after the API returns. When provisioning finishes, the slot is released even though the cluster may continue running customer workloads. The controller counts active provisioning workflows; it does not count all running clusters or allocated VMs and vCPUs. Tracking a slot does not require holding a thread.

When a cloud provider slows down, provisioning workflows hold their slots longer and accepted requests wait longer to launch. The controller also reduces the slot limit when congestion signals, such as provisioning latency or thread pool saturation, indicate pressure. As conditions recover, it cautiously allows more concurrent work.

The fixed API request-rate limit protects against exceptionally high incoming traffic and provides a request-rate boundary we can communicate to customers. Adaptive concurrency limits work inside the service: capacity pressure queues accepted requests and delays provisioning. A successful API response does not guarantee an immediate cluster launch or completion within a fixed time.

The initial rollout analysis reported 7.5× higher default cluster-creation request-rate limits, more than 99.99% fewer cluster-creation rate-limit errors in the reported scope, and removal of over a hundred customer-specific rate-limit overrides in scope. Since the increase, few customers have hit the higher limits, and no new manual overrides have been added for those limits.

For the complementary problem of enforcing API quotas at scale, read High Performance Ratelimiting at Databricks.

entries.content:
A field guide to Lakebase branching, reverse ETL, and real-time serving, told through eleven customer projects

by Shruti Prasanna, Nikhil Tallam and Rob Bajra

  • Our latest customer hackathon put Databricks Lakebase in the spotlight, and the eleven projects show the full range of what a Postgres database built for the lakehouse can do.
  • The two tracks line up with two ways teams use Lakebase: building applications on it with database branching, and connecting it to the lakehouse to serve data and ML features in real time.
  • From AI agents that test their actions on a branch before touching production to an insurer retiring a separate search index, the builds show why the operational database is becoming part of the data platform instead of a system that sits next to it.

We run these hackathons for a simple reason: the fastest way to learn a product is to build something with it. Each one starts with an enablement session where teams learn the product and where it’s headed on the roadmap. Then the building starts. Teams work together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes.

This time, we opened the hackathon to a much wider group of customers than ever before, and the product in the spotlight was Databricks Lakebase.

Lakebase is fully managed Postgres, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away. What makes it different is what sits underneath. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance. That opens up three things a typical Postgres database can’t do as easily:

  • Branch it. Lakebase branches work like Git branches for your database. A new branch is created instantly using copy-on-write storage, so you only pay for the data that changes, and creating one has no performance impact on production.
  • Sync it. Synced tables continuously copy Unity Catalog tables into Postgres as read-only tables, so applications can query lakehouse data with low latency. This is commonly called reverse ETL. In the other direction, Lakehouse Sync replicates Postgres tables back into Unity Catalog Delta tables using change data capture.
  • Serve it. Lakebase can hold application state, power search with extensions like pgvector, PostGIS, and pg_trgm, and act as the online store behind Databricks Online Feature Stores for real-time ML.

Those map to the two tracks we ran. Track 1 focused on branching and building applications. Track 2 focused on syncing and serving. Underneath both, Unity Catalog governs who can see what, whether the data is being queried in a notebook or read by a production app.

Who it’s for: application developers. These are the engineers who build the apps, APIs, and agents that run on operational data, and who have usually had to choose between a slow, shared staging database and an expensive copy for every developer. Branching removes that tradeoff. Every Lakebase project starts with a production branch, and you can create child branches from it for development, testing, or experiments. Because branches use copy-on-write, a branch of a large database is ready in seconds, and only the changes take up new storage. Teams in this track used Genie Code to build their apps and treated branches as cheap, disposable copies of production.

Lyft took on a problem that’s growing as AI agents start acting on production data: agents that issue refunds, cancel bookings, or close tickets without knowing the business rules that live inside the database as triggers. Their project, Jevons Search, gives the agent a Lakebase branch to work on. For each batch of support tickets, the agent forks a copy-on-write branch of production in about six seconds, applies its actions, reads back what the database actually did, and adjusts. Instead of using a large LLM to plan, a lightweight classifier built on gte-large embeddings, tracked in MLflow, and served on Model Serving sorts each ticket into one of eight policy categories, with no LLM tokens used at runtime. On a synthetic dataset built from the Wanderbricks sample data, planning up front fully resolved 2 of 11 support backlogs within policy. Testing on branches resolved 10 of 11. The team also tested the idea behind the project’s name: Lakebase forked fast enough to score more than four times as many branches in the same minute, but more branches didn’t lead to more passes. Precise decisions plus real feedback from the database beat brute force.

CIBC built Branchflight, a platform that gives every pull request its own preview environment. When a pull request opens, Branchflight creates a zero-copy Lakebase branch from a PII-masked template branch in under five seconds and deploys a preview Databricks App connected to it. Environments scale to zero when no one is using them, expire automatically after a set time, and pass through a schema-diff check before changes merge. The platform’s own state, audit logs, and cost metrics live in Lakebase too.

Arbital Health asked a question every team putting text-to-SQL in front of users should think about: how much does the schema itself affect accuracy? Their benchmark, 7NF, keeps the data fixed and changes the schema, with each layout running as its own Lakebase branch. Models are graded only on whether they return the correct rows, so teams can pick the best schema for a customer database or improve their own text-to-SQL models.

Branching also showed up in some unexpected places.

For their hackathon submission, OneTrust brought Lakebase branching to network security by treating firewall rules like code. To evaluate proposed changes without risk to live infrastructure, they experimented with having a Go app spin up a copy-on-write Lakebase branch with dedicated compute and connect a test instance to run recursive reachability queries and policy checks. In testing, trial runs that expanded the attack surface were discarded instantly, while validated rules merged directly into production.

A second CIBC team built BranchCut, a 3D cinematic workspace that brings Git-style branching and merging to creative work. Creators branch from any point in a scene, try different camera moves or lighting, compare versions side by side, and merge the best one back, with Lakebase tracking projects, branches, scene state, and merge history.

Reach Mobile built StreetCart, which helps shoppers compare nearby stores on price, distance, and stock instead of walking store to store. Lakebase is the app’s operational database for products, stores, and inventory, and Lakebase search powers product discovery. The team used branching to test new product category attributes before changing the production schema.

Markel went after a system most property and casualty insurers run: a separate search index, often Elasticsearch, kept only so claims, underwriting, and call center teams get fast reads. That second copy has its own pipeline, its own schema drift, and its own governance gaps. Markel’s app serves those reads from the same governed gold tables used for analytics, through Lakebase. Claims analysts search for policies by number, name, address, or phone; call center agents identify callers by phone number across policy, claims, and broker data; and underwriters see loss runs for a broker in one place. New claims are scored for risk as they arrive.

Building on Lakebase is only half the story. The other half is what happens when the operational database and the lakehouse stop being separate systems.

Who it’s for: data and ML engineers. These are the people who build the pipelines and models, and who usually have to build a separate path to get that data into the apps and services that need it in milliseconds.

This track was about closing that gap. Synced tables move curated Unity Catalog data into Lakebase Postgres through managed Spark Declarative Pipelines, so apps can join it with their own tables. Lakebase Change Data Feed goes the other way and streams changes made in Postgres back to Delta for analytics. And because Databricks Online Feature Stores run on Lakebase, features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time.

Data Axle built PriceWise for vacation rental hosts who set one flat nightly price while demand changes dramatically across the year. Across more than 18,000 listings, the team estimated hosts leave about 64% of potential nightly revenue on the table. PriceWise combines hybrid search (pgvector embeddings plus BM25, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion), pricing suggestions broken down into four demand drivers including PostGIS comparisons of listings within 20 miles, and an embedded Genie agent that answers questions like which amenities top competitors have. Every Genie conversation is saved in Lakebase as agent memory, so hosts can pick up where they left off. Search, pricing, agent memory, and feature serving all run from one Lakebase database kept current through synced tables, with pricing responses in as little as 4 milliseconds, and host decisions written back to Lakebase.

A team from a transportation company built a real-time flight risk app that turns streaming data into a live operational view. They synced flight, airport, and weather alert tables from Unity Catalog into Lakebase to power a live map in a Databricks App, showing how synced tables let the same pipelines that feed analytics feed an operational app.

Another team from an insurance company focused on a gap that comes after a policy is issued. Risk scoring usually happens before a policy is bound, but no one predicts what the inspector will find afterward. Their app scores how likely each post-bind inspection is to lead to carrier action and ranks the inspection queue so the riskiest policies are seen first, with plain-language reasons. Features are defined once as Databricks Feature Views and served from a Lakebase online store, so the same definitions power training and real-time scoring.

Sobeys built a conversational shopping assistant with three agents. A recipe agent finds recipes with Vector Search, a product agent matches ingredients to store products using fuzzy Postgres trigram search, and a health agent checks every recipe against the family’s allergy profiles. Ask for Thai recipes that are safe for a peanut allergy, and the app goes from recipe to ingredients to cart in one conversation.

Read the two tracks back to back and you get a working tour of Lakebase. A developer gives an AI agent a branch instead of production. A platform team gives every pull request its own database in seconds. A data engineer syncs curated tables into Postgres to power a live app. An ML engineer defines features once and serves them in real time.

What ties all of it together is that Lakebase doesn’t sit apart from the data platform. The same Unity Catalog governance applies to the lakehouse tables and the Postgres tables that serve them, and the same data that powers a dashboard can power an app, an agent, or a model. Several teams replaced a separate system, like a search index, a staging database, or a hand-built sync job, with something Lakebase handles directly.

Hats off to all eleven teams for building something real. A few resources to get started with Lakebase:

Lakebase is fully managed Postgres built for the lakehouse. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away.

Lakebase branches work like Git branches for your database. Every project starts with a production branch, and new child branches are created instantly using copy-on-write storage, so you only pay for the data that changes and creating a branch has no performance impact on production.

Yes. Lakebase supports Postgres extensions like pgvector, PostGIS, and pg_trgm for search, and it acts as the online store behind Databricks Online Feature Stores, so features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time.

Each hackathon starts with an enablement session on the product and its roadmap. Teams then build together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes. This Lakebase hackathon had two tracks and eleven customer projects.

  • New to Lakebase? Start with the Lakebase product page and the docs on branches.
  • Want to bring lakehouse data into your app? Read about synced tables and Lakehouse Sync.
  • Building search or real-time ML? See the supported Postgres extensions and Lakebase-powered Online Feature Stores.
  • Ready to try it? Start a free trial and create your first Lakebase project.

entries.content:
The modern Databricks Data + AI Platform, with Unity Catalog and serverless compute, now available for the missions that matter most.

by Rory Patterson, Filippo Seracini and Vijay Raja

  • Azure Databricks on Azure Government is now in Beta. It brings the same modern data foundation as commercial Azure Databricks, so government teams can work the way their commercial peers do.
  • Agencies can govern, analyze and secure data from day one. They get Unity Catalog governance, serverless analytics with Databricks SQL, secure-by-default workspaces, and U.S.-only data residency in US Gov Virginia and US Gov Arizona.
  • AI is next, and so is the compliance path. Genie, Agent Bricks, Model Serving and more are planned on the way to General Availability, along with FedRAMP Class D and IL5 authorization expected by early 2027.

Government agencies and their mission-critical partners face a persistent dilemma: adopt the latest data and AI innovations, or meet the stringent security and compliance requirements their missions demand. For too long, these have been competing priorities, forcing public sector organizations to operate on platforms that lag behind their commercial counterparts, sometimes by years.

Today, we're excited to announce that Azure Databricks on Azure Government is entering Beta, a major milestone in our commitment to delivering the full power of the Databricks Data + AI Platform to the U.S. public sector. Government agencies and the hundreds of organizations that support them now have access to the modern data foundation already transforming industries across the commercial sector, including Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, and serverless compute, with the complete suite of AI capabilities to follow, all within an environment working toward FedRAMP Class D (formerly “High”) and DoW IL5 authorization.

Databricks recently launched the FedRAMP Class D offering on Azure Commercial. And today we are bringing the best of Databricks to Azure Government, so U.S. public sector customers now have a modern Databricks platform on both Azure clouds.

For federal civilian agencies, state and local governments, and partners whose workloads fit FedRAMP Class D, Azure Commercial is available today. For organizations that need a dedicated government cloud and a path to FedRAMP Class D and DoW IL5, the new Azure Government environment is now open for Beta.

As a first-party Azure service, Azure Databricks is managed through the Azure portal, integrates natively with Microsoft Entra ID, and counts toward existing Azure commitments, so agencies can adopt it inside the cloud, contracts, and identity systems they already trust.

Unlike the legacy environment, the new Azure Databricks on Azure Government runs on the same architecture as commercial Azure Databricks. It is designed to receive the full Databricks platform, with every commercial feature coming to Azure Government through the same ongoing releases. Beta is the first release on that path, and it already gives government teams the core capabilities their commercial peers rely on.

  • One place to govern data and AI. For the first time on Azure Government, Unity Catalog lets teams manage access, track lineage, and audit usage across all data and AI assets. Define a policy once, apply it everywhere, and easily show who accessed what, when, and why.
  • Analytics without infrastructure overhead. Databricks SQL delivers fast, high-concurrency analytics. Engineers and data scientists can choose classic clusters or serverless compute for each workload, which means less time sizing and patching clusters and more time delivering for the mission.
  • Secure by default. Every workspace comes with the Compliance Security Profile already enabled. It provides enhanced monitoring, automatic cluster updates, a hardened compute image, and encrypted traffic between cluster nodes. Azure Private Link is required on the front end and back end, so all traffic stays on the Azure backbone.
  • Full visibility into usage and spend. System tables give administrators one queryable view of audit logs, billing, compute, pipelines, ML experiments, query history, and storage, so they can answer audit requests and manage costs with familiar tools.
  • Data stays in government regions. Customer content is stored and processed only in U.S. government cloud regions: US Gov Virginia and US Gov Arizona.

Beta lays the governed, secure foundation that AI depends on. Next, we'll bring the full Databricks AI suite to Azure Government, all governed by Unity Catalog, so every model, agent, and answer inherits the same access controls, lineage, and auditing as the underlying data. On the roadmap:

  • Conversational analytics with Genie. Ask questions in plain language and get accurate, governed answers, with no SQL and no waiting on a reporting queue.
  • AI-assisted development. Built-in AI helps engineers, analysts, and data scientists write, explain, and debug code faster.
  • Production-grade agents with Agent Bricks. Build, evaluate, and deploy agents that reason over your own documents and data, for example to search case files, summarize reports, or automate routine workflows. Built-in quality evaluation means teams can trust the results before putting them in front of users.
  • Models and serving. Model Serving and Foundation Model APIs let teams deploy their own models and use curated foundation models through a single governed endpoint.
  • AI on all your data. Vector Search and AI Functions power retrieval-augmented apps and let teams classify, extract, and summarize data directly in SQL, without moving it.
  • Data and AI applications. Databricks Apps and Lakebase let teams build secure, interactive applications and operational workloads directly on the lakehouse.

Roadmap capabilities and timelines are forward-looking and subject to change.

Databricks is actively pursuing FedRAMP Class D (formerly FedRAMP High) and DoW Impact Level 5 (IL5) authorizations for the new Azure Government environment, expected in early 2027. Once authorized, agencies and defense partners will be able to run Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and mission-critical workloads on the modern Databricks platform, including the defense workloads that require IL5 and are not supported on Azure Commercial.

Track our authorization progress on the FedRAMP Marketplace.

New to the environment? Opt in with a dedicated Azure Government subscription that has never been used for Azure Databricks. After you register the new-environment preview feature in the Azure portal, every new workspace in that subscription is created in the new environment. During Beta, the environment is intended for non-production workloads. The workspaces you build now will carry forward to production at General Availability.

Already on the legacy Azure Government environment? Now is the time to start planning your migration. Your existing workspaces, notebooks, data, and configurations are unaffected, so you can explore the new environment side by side and work out your path forward. We recommend starting with four areas:

  • Unity Catalog. Legacy Azure Government workspaces have never had Unity Catalog. Starting early gives your teams time to design and adopt unified governance.
  • Serverless compute. Serverless is new to government environments, so begin your internal security and compliance review now.
  • Network encryption. The Compliance Security Profile is enabled on every workspace and requires instance types that support Azure Virtual Network encryption. Update your cluster configurations and Terraform/ARM templates to match.
  • Your ATO. Start working with your security and authorizing officials now to add Databricks on Azure Government to your system's Authorization to Operate. Updating system security plans, data flows, and boundary documentation during Beta puts you in a position to run CUI production workloads at General Availability, expected in early 2027.

Our Federal team can help you assess your workloads and plan the move.

entries.content:
Learn how Databricks and Google are advancing interoperability through open standards.

by Alex Jiang, Parth Desai and John Spencer

  • Customers can access the same copy of data from either BigQuery or Databricks without duplication.
  • Google and Databricks are committed to a long-term vision of shared catalog metadata.

The Lakehouse architecture is becoming more open than ever. What started with open table formats – Delta Lake and Iceberg – has evolved into catalog federation for zero-copy access across multiple platforms. Through our partnership and Open Source contributions, Databricks and Google Cloud continue to drive advancements in the Open Lakehouse community.

Today, we're proud to announce a significant milestone in catalog interoperability in collaboration with Google: customers can now access a single copy of data from both Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse. The Databricks and Google Cloud partnership continues to thrive, and we're committed to making bi-directional interoperability seamless.

Bringing data from Google Cloud into Databricks is simple. With Lakehouse Federation to Google Cloud, now generally available, customers can mount Iceberg tables managed by Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog in Unity Catalog for analysis in Databricks.

These Iceberg tables from Google's Lakehouse runtime catalog can then be queried by Databricks Lakehouse, our serverless data warehouse, or analyzed via Genie, which intelligently answers data questions from natural language – no code or SQL required.

Interoperability works in the other direction as well. Data from Databricks can also be brought into Google Cloud's Lakehouse (learn more). This allows customers using engines like BigQuery to read Unity Catalog managed tables without data copy.

Databricks and Google Cloud are taking major strides to strengthen interoperability by making catalog metadata open. Our belief is that business and governance semantics should be accessible rather than tied to a specific vendor. In the Iceberg community, we helped drive and land catalog labels - a proposal that enables catalogs to share metadata through key-value pairs (a.k.a labels). That way, a table tagged as "domain=finance" and "status=certified" with a column tagged as "pii=ssn" continues to be tagged even as the table is federated from one catalog to another (learn more).

Shared labels are critical for governance in the era of agents as catalog metadata can be used to flag sensitive data for masking and provide context to agents searching for assets to answer data questions. Through our partnership, Databricks and Google Cloud are committed to advancing the vision of open governance. As data estates grow and AI agents become more embedded in enterprise workflows, that shared commitment becomes increasingly important. We're headed towards a future where governance and business context can travel with data without requiring enterprises to redefine them in every system.

Get started with Catalog Federation between Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse by reading our documentation. You can also learn more about Google's catalog federation to Unity Catalog here.

If you're interested in sharing your interoperability needs or learning more about our vision for interoperability, please reach out to your Databricks account team.
